newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: RTRS-Malaysia's Petronas sees rich returns in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Malaysia's Petronas sees rich returns in Vietnam.

text.p: Malaysia's state-owned Petroliam Nasional (Petronas) is moving to increase commercial ties with Vietnam -- a country it sees providing rich returns in the future -- even as other companies are pulling out, analysts say.
Petronas said on Tuesday it had agreed to take over Vietnam's controversial Dai Hung oilfield, once seen as a giant reservior of black gold but now viewed as providing marginal profits at best.

Analysts said behind the move was Petronas's international push to not only increase sales from outside Malaysia but to further integrate itself into a country that potentially shows explosive double-digit energy demand growth in the years ahead.
"Its 77 million people are very rapidly entering the modern world and they will need energy fairly quickly," said Al Troner, managing director of Asia Pacific Energy Consulting.
A Petronas spokesman said the company bought a 43.75 percent stake in Dai Hung from Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) of Australia. That takes Petronas's total holding to 63.75 percent.
BHP, which declined to comment, had been trying for more than a year to negotiate more favourable terms with the Vietnam government to exploit the oilfield.
PetroVietnam said the Petronas announcement was premature and government approval was still needed.
A consortium led by BHP signed a production-sharing contract with Vietnam in 1993 for Dai Hung, when the field was touted as the biggest in Vietnam with 700 million barrels of recoverable reserves.

The estimates have since crumbled and analysts now say the field, once thought to be the largest in Asia, has 100 million barrels of recoverable reserves at best. Some estimates run as low as 75 million barrels.

BHP's departure from the field follows a string of similar moves by oil firms. Total SA of France in 1995 pulled out of a high-profile $1.2 billion project to build Vietnam's first refinery, saying the project was not economically viable.
Royal Dutch Shell, the Anglo-Dutch oil giant, failed to renew a production sharing contract with Vietnam last year after "taking a more realistic view of Vietnam".
Analysts said the major problem for many of the companies has simply been that projects failed to live up to expectations or pricing terms were not what they had expected.
"A lot of these companies, like Shell and BHP, have a lot more pressure from shareholders on whether to invest in something that is not going to make money," one analyst said.
But Petronas does not have such immediate pressures.
Vietnam offers potentially bigger growth for energy producers than other Asian countries, including South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia because of its larger population.
It already has a 15-percent stake in the refinery project, which is yet to be built, is trying to develop retail gasoline outlets and has interest in other crude fields.
So increasing involvement with Dai Hung will deepen ties with Vietnam -- even if the field is not a clear profit maker.
"They are willing to take less than commercial rates of return to develop a longer term commercial relationship," Troner said.
Petronas President Hassan Marican told The Eagle financial weekly that the field was a risk worth taking.
"It will be tough, but I believe we can make money," he said.
Petronas is looking to diversify internationally and has set a target of generating one third of consolidated turnover outside Malaysia by 2005.
